title: How Vaccines Train the Immune System — Place the Missing Sentences

prompt: Six sentences have been removed from this article. Place each missing sentence into the gap where it best fits. There is one extra sentence you do not need.
passage:
When a vaccine enters the body, it carries a harmless version of the pathogen — a fragment of protein, a weakened virus, or a strand of genetic instructions. @@@1 The immune system, never having seen the real pathogen, treats this rehearsal as a genuine threat and mobilises its defences. White blood cells called B-cells produce antibodies that lock onto the foreign material, while T-cells learn to recognise infected cells and destroy them.

@@@2 These memory cells circulate at low levels for years, sometimes decades. If the real pathogen ever arrives, the response that took two weeks the first time can be completed in two days. @@@3

Not every vaccine works the same way. Live attenuated vaccines use a weakened form of the original microbe and tend to produce strong, long-lasting immunity. @@@4 Subunit and mRNA vaccines, by contrast, present only a fragment of the pathogen — usually a single surface protein — and so cannot cause the disease at all. @@@5

Vaccine effectiveness is rarely all-or-nothing. @@@6 This is why outbreaks can still occur in vaccinated populations, although the illness is usually milder and the chain of transmission is shorter. The point of vaccination is not to make every individual immune in isolation; it is to raise the population's collective resistance high enough that the pathogen cannot spread freely.

placements.item: This decoy presents the immune system with a kind of training exercise.
Crucially, after the threat is cleared, a small population of B-cells and T-cells is preserved as memory.
That speed is the difference between a brief, mild infection and a serious illness.
However, because the microbe is still alive, they are not usually given to people whose immune systems are compromised.
The trade-off is that they often need a booster dose to maintain protection over time.
Even a successful vaccine typically reduces, rather than abolishes, the chance of infection.

distractors: Antibiotics, unlike vaccines, treat infections after they have already taken hold.
